headline: New 30% CGT floor will push low-income and early-retirement investors to realise gains sooner and redirect capital toward income assets
reasoning: Robert Zammit explains that the proposed 30% minimum tax rate on real capital gains prevents investors from timing when they realise gains to hit a lower marginal rate. Clients expecting to be below 30% in future years are accelerating gain realisation in the current year while their tax rate is still lower. Early retirees who planned to draw down investment portfolios gradually before accessing superannuation will be disproportionately affected. Part-time workers, students and young investors in shares or crypto are also caught. The only exemptions apply to means-tested income recipients such as age pension, disability pension and jobseeker recipients.
quote: These changes are really designed to make sure that these gains are taxed at 30% as a minimum. Now people will be paying a higher rate of tax if their marginal tax rate is higher. But really it's stopping people the ability to control when they realize these taxes. So it's going to affect a lot of retirees, um, and low income earners... Young people trying to get ahead. Most definitely think part time workers, you know, studying. And then maybe they're saving and investing in some shares or cryptocurrency. Um, they've been caught up in this. And they'll find that they're paying a higher tax rate than what they would otherwise.

headline: Low-marginal-rate investors should consider shifting from capital-growth to income-focused assets including cash, term deposits and fixed interest under new CGT rules
reasoning: Zammit argues that the 30% minimum tax applies only to real capital gains, not to income returns such as dividends, rent and interest, which remain taxed at the individual's marginal rate. For investors whose marginal rate is below 30%, income-oriented investments become relatively more tax-efficient than growth assets. He outlines a risk spectrum from cash and term deposits through government and private credit fixed interest up to commercial or office property, all of which offer higher income yields than capital appreciation. His personal view is that high-marginal-rate investors should still pursue capital growth, but low-rate investors have an incentive to tilt toward income.
quote: People who have lower marginal tax rates, lower than the 30%, might want to shift how they're investing their money. And that's because it's the only the capital gains, the real capital gains that will be taxed at 30%. Whilst if you look at income returns, think rent, dividends, interest, that's not going to be taxed at the minimum 30% capital gain... People might think, oh, I'm better off just focusing on income investments. I'm going to be taxed less on them and that they're safe and easier to achieve... Cash term deposits obviously the safer ones. And then you can go into the fixed interest space. And in there you can have a mixture of either government lending or private credit lending... even if we get into the property market and we start looking there, people might shift their allocations to more like commercial or office based investments rather than residential, as they're all known to pay higher income yields than capital appreciation.
